strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and relatively underexplored problem: automatically creating instance-level, physics-enabled tabletop scenes from text or a single image. The resulting scenes have clear potential for embodied-AI simulation and content creation.

TabletopGen is a coherent end-to-end system combining instance completion, per-object 3D generation, canonicalization, pose estimation, metric scaling, and Isaac Sim assembly. The decomposition into Differentiable Rotation Optimization (DRO) and Top-view Spatial Alignment (TSA) is intuitive and practically motivated.

The visual results are generally impressive and show diverse table shapes, object categories, styles, real-image inputs, and instance-level editing. Comparisons suggest substantially better object completeness and fewer visible placement failures than ACDC, Gen3DSR, and MIDI.

The evaluation includes complementary perceptual metrics, collision statistics, component ablations, a 128-participant user study, runtime analysis, prompts, intermediate outputs, and robotic-manipulation demonstrations. In particular, the large reductions in object- and scene-level collision rates are practically meaningful.

The manuscript is well organized, and the supplementary material provides useful implementation details and illustrates the intermediate representations, evaluation interface, and camera-sweep protocol.
weaknesses: The central claim of precise 3D pose, scale, and layout recovery is not directly evaluated. LPIPS, DINOv2, and CLIP on the best of 160 rendered views measure appearance agreement but can hide geometric errors; collision rates measure only one aspect of physical validity. Ground-truth rotation, translation, scale, support-relation, object-count, and layout errors on a synthetic or annotated benchmark are needed to validate DRO and TSA.

TSA derives geometry from a generated top-view image rather than observed evidence. A generative model is explicitly asked to retain every object's position, orientation, and aspect ratio, but no experiment establishes that it does so. Hallucination or displacement in this image is consequently converted directly into the reconstructed layout. Likewise, metric scale depends on MLLM-guessed commonsense sizes and a single anchor, with no quantitative scale-accuracy or sensitivity analysis.

The evaluation set of 78 samples is insufficiently specified: its source, text/image split, proportion of real photographs, prompt construction, and public availability are unclear. If references were synthesized using the same Seedream model also used for completion and top-view generation, the large gains may partly reflect a favorable, internally consistent generation domain rather than general single-image reconstruction. Real-world evidence is limited to two qualitative examples.

Baseline coverage and comparison protocols are not fully convincing. Highly relevant cited compositional/layout-alignment systems such as Reparo are omitted, MesaTask is compared on only a small qualitative example, and it is unclear whether every baseline received equivalent camera optimization and postprocessing. Statistical uncertainty across the 78 scenes is not reported.

The component analysis replaces DRO or TSA only with an MLLM estimate. It does not isolate the proposed loss terms, anchor score, generated top view, commonsense-size prior, camera estimate, or generative completion. Consequently, the experiments show that the overall stages help but do not establish which technical choices are responsible or whether simpler geometric alternatives would suffice.

The stated simulation-readiness and robot-policy-learning impact is overclaimed relative to the evidence. The paper reports residual scene collisions, assigns generic gravity and friction, and gives only two successful hand-selected manipulation demonstrations. It does not evaluate stability after settling, mass/friction realism, collision-mesh quality, articulation, graspability, task success rates, or actual policy training and transfer.

Reproducibility depends heavily on external and partly proprietary models. The main paper says only 'ChatGPT' despite using it for several consequential vision and reasoning stages, and stochastic-generation settings, API/model versions, retry policies, failure handling, and total API cost are not adequately documented. Code is only promised for future release.

DRO optimizes only vertical-axis rotation after MLLM-based canonicalization and camera prediction. The method therefore inherits unmeasured errors from both preceding steps and is not evidently robust to non-upright, symmetric, heavily occluded, or incorrectly completed objects. Broader failure-case and robustness analyses are absent.

The user study is sizable but lacks confidence intervals, significance testing, participant demographics, and analysis controlling for repeated ratings. GPT-4o evaluation is also potentially correlated with the ChatGPT-based design choices and should not be treated as independent evidence. These limitations make the reported preference margins harder to interpret rigorously.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision and embodied-AI problem: automatically constructing editable, instance-level tabletop scenes rather than producing only a monolithic visual representation.

The overall pipeline is coherent, and decomposing alignment into differentiable yaw optimization (DRO) and top-view-based translation/scale estimation (TSA) is intuitive. Per-instance assets also naturally support editing and physical interaction.

The qualitative results are visually strong, and the reported collision rates substantially improve over the evaluated baselines. The paper includes component ablations, a 126-response user study, efficiency measurements, prompts, intermediate outputs, and two manipulation demonstrations.

I assess this primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution, despite no declared type. weaknesses: The central geometric claims are not directly validated. There is no ground-truth evaluation of rotation, translation, scale, object support, floating, or physical stability. Image similarity, collision counts, GPT-4o judgments, and user preference cannot establish that the method accurately recovers 3D pose or metric scale.

TSA depends on a generative model hallucinating an orthographic top view while preserving every object's position and orientation. The prompt requests this behavior, but no consistency guarantee or empirical accuracy analysis is provided. Metric scale is then inferred from fallible MLLM commonsense dimensions and a single selected anchor. The derivation of per-axis scales and propagation of uncertainty are also insufficiently specified.

The evaluation is heavily synthetic and potentially favorable to the proposed pipeline: most of the 78 references appear to be generated by the same Seedream model used for completion and top-view synthesis. Generalization to actual photographs is supported only by two qualitative examples, making the claimed real-to-sim capability unconvincing.

The visual-metric protocol selects the best among 160 rendered views independently for each result and metric. This removes the need to recover the input camera and introduces a substantial multiple-comparison advantage; it therefore does not cleanly measure reconstruction or alignment accuracy. No fixed-camera or calibrated-camera results are reported.

The comparison set is incomplete for a state-of-the-art claim. Closely related compositional/alignment approaches such as Reparo and CAST are cited but not evaluated. Text-to-scene performance is compared with only MesaTask, qualitatively, despite text input being a headline capability. Baseline configurations and efforts to ensure comparable assets and rendering are not documented sufficiently.

The claimed “collision-free” guarantee is contradicted by the reported 7.69% scene collision rate—approximately 6 of 78 scenes. Collision checks alone also omit floating objects, unstable support, center-of-mass feasibility, frictional stability, and behavior under perturbation. Two scripted manipulation demonstrations are too limited to establish suitability for policy learning or robust embodied interaction.

The ablations replace DRO or TSA with a weak MLLM-only alternative, but do not isolate the proposed loss terms, camera estimation, generative top-view step, commonsense-size estimates, or RMA anchor selection. No oracle or ground-truth-pose experiments reveal which stage actually determines accuracy or where errors accumulate.

Statistical reporting is inadequate: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, per-category breakdowns, failure analysis, or repeated-run analysis for stochastic and API-based components. GPT-4o evaluation details are insufficient, while the human study reports only aggregate means despite repeated observations per participant.

Reproducibility is limited by unreleased code, a blank project-page entry, proprietary ChatGPT and Seedream dependencies, missing API versions/settings/seeds, and an apparent inconsistency between the stated Hunyuan3D-3.0 implementation and the Hunyuan3D-2.5 reference. Given these concerns, the impressive qualitative presentation does not yet support the paper's strong accuracy, generalization, and simulation-readiness claims.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper addresses a practically important and relatively underserved computer-vision problem: producing instance-level, physically interactive tabletop scenes from text or a single image, with clear relevance to embodied AI and robot manipulation.

The overall system is coherent and technically well motivated. Per-instance completion and 3D generation address occlusion and asset-library limitations, while the two-stage alignment design sensibly separates yaw recovery through differentiable rendering (DRO) from translation and metric-scale estimation through top-view reasoning (TSA).

The empirical results are strong and consistent across complementary measures. On 78 test scenes, TabletopGen improves LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP, GPT-4o judgments, and collision statistics over ACDC, Gen3DSR, and MIDI; the reduction in object-pair collision rate from 8.23–17.39% to 0.42% is particularly compelling for the intended application.

The ablations support the value of both main alignment components: removing DRO increases scene-level collisions from 7.69% to 16.67%, while removing TSA raises them to 61.54%. The qualitative examples also clearly illustrate the associated rotation and placement failures.

The human evaluation is substantial, with 126 retained participants and randomized presentation. TabletopGen receives markedly higher fidelity, alignment, and physical-plausibility ratings and 83.13% overall preference, reinforcing the automated results.

The presentation is clear and visually effective. The supplement provides intermediate outputs, prompts, runtime breakdowns, evaluation details, real-image and stylized examples, scene editing, and two manipulation demonstrations. The modular outputs and promised code release could make the system useful to the community.
weaknesses: The central geometric evidence remains indirect. No dataset with ground-truth object rotations, metric scales, translations, support relations, or reconstructed geometry is used, so the paper does not directly establish the accuracy of DRO or TSA. The reported image-similarity metrics select an oracle best view from 160 renders and can conceal incorrect geometry, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

TSA relies on a generative model to hallucinate an orthographic top view and on an MLLM to infer physical dimensions and stacking. These outputs need not preserve the input layout. The paper lacks controlled measurements of top-view fidelity, anchor-selection failures, size-prior errors, or sensitivity to the RMA tolerance, and the ablation does not isolate these subcomponents.

The evaluation set is only loosely documented. Its 78 references appear to include model-generated images, but the paper does not report the exact source distribution, text-versus-real-image breakdown, selection procedure, object-density statistics, or category splits. Only a few real-world examples are shown, limiting support for broad real-to-sim and generalization claims.

The text-to-scene capability is evaluated against MesaTask only through two qualitative examples. Consequently, the evidence primarily supports single-image reconstruction rather than the full unified text-or-image claim.

The phrase “simulation-ready” is stronger than the validation. Convex collision proxies, gravity, and friction are assigned, but there is no systematic evaluation of stability after simulation, contact quality, mass/inertia, mesh defects, graspability, or downstream policy performance. Only two scripted manipulation demonstrations are reported, and 7.69% of generated scenes still contain a collision.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on closed and potentially changing ChatGPT and Seedream services. Exact model snapshots, decoding settings, retry policies, failure handling, and monetary/API costs are not specified; the cited Hunyuan reference also appears to describe version 2.5 while the implementation names Hunyuan3D-3.0.

The user and GPT-based studies omit confidence intervals or significance tests, per-scene variance, evaluator agreement, and sufficient GPT-evaluation configuration details. These omissions do not negate the unusually large observed margins, but they make the strength and repeatability of those comparisons harder to assess.

DRO optimizes only rotation around the vertical axis after an MLLM-based canonicalization step, restricting applicability to upright objects. Failure cases involving tilted, articulated, severely occluded, transparent, reflective, or very small objects are not systematically analyzed.

strengths: The paper presents a useful end-to-end system that converts text or a single image into instance-separated, physics-enabled tabletop scenes. Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, Applied/Systems is more appropriate than Algorithms/General; under that framing, the integration of asset generation, alignment, collision construction, simulation, editing, and trajectory synthesis is a meaningful contribution.

The tabletop-specific decomposition is sensible. DRO estimates yaw using complementary silhouette, edge, and appearance signals, while TSA introduces support relations, tabletop boundaries, and a metric-scale anchor. The component ablations show that both stages contribute, with TSA especially important for reducing collisions.

Evaluation covers several relevant dimensions: perceptual similarity, mesh collisions, support and settling stability, human judgments, qualitative comparisons, and downstream robot experiments. The reported physical improvements are large: 0.42% colliding pairs, 7.69% scenes with collisions, 100% support stability, and 92.13% dynamic settling stability on the stated test set.

The real-robot study is valuable evidence beyond rendering quality: policies trained from 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task achieve 84%, 80%, and 68% success over 50 real trials. The supplementary material also provides stage-wise outputs, prompts, test-set composition, camera-sweep details, and user-study procedures.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and candid about its current restriction to conventional tabletop settings.
weaknesses: The central TSA procedure is insufficiently specified for reproduction. The paper does not give complete algorithms for converting generated top-view boxes and MLLM-proposed object sizes into per-axis scales, deciding when an object is rescaled, resolving inconsistent sizes or supports, or handling uncertainty. The supplement even states that objects with substantial size deviations are rescaled without defining the rule. Reproducibility is further limited by dependence on closed or rapidly changing ChatGPT and Seedream services, with no runtime, cost, model snapshot, or failure/retry information.

The evaluation does not directly substantiate the claimed layout accuracy. There are no ground-truth translation, rotation, scale, support-relation, object-recall, or boundary-containment errors. LPIPS/DINO/CLIP are computed after independently selecting the best of 160 rendered views, which can absorb camera and geometry errors and is not a direct reconstruction metric. The very large GPT-4o scores are also hard to interpret because the evaluator prompt, repeated-query protocol, variance, and possible model-family bias are not reported.

Generalization evidence is limited: 74 of the 78 evaluation inputs are synthetic and only four are real photographs. The synthetic images are generated in a controlled style closely aligned with the proposed pipeline, which also uses generative image models for completion and top-view synthesis. More varied real imagery, severe occlusion, transparent or reflective objects, clutter, unusual supports, and explicit failure rates are needed.

The physical-usability claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Collision and five-second settling tests do not establish graspability, accurate mass/friction/contact properties, or motion-planning success. How physical parameters and collision decompositions are selected is largely unspecified. Holodeck-table's zero collision rate also illustrates that collision metrics alone can reward sparse or trivial layouts.

The real-to-sim-to-real result is promising but narrow: it uses one reconstructed tabletop, three related pick-and-place/stacking tasks, and one robot setup, without comparisons to alternative scene reconstruction, simpler domain-randomized simulation, or policy training without TabletopGen. Thus it demonstrates feasibility rather than isolating the system's causal benefit or supporting broad data-engine claims.

The user study lacks confidence intervals, significance tests, participant demographics, and analysis accounting for multiple ratings from each participant. Likewise, most quantitative tables report only means, without uncertainty across scenes. The ablation replaces modules with an MLLM-only baseline but does not isolate the contributions of the RMA anchor, generated top view, stacking inference, individual DRO losses, or camera-pose estimation.

Algorithmic originality is moderate: DRO largely combines established differentiable-rendering losses, while TSA relies heavily on generated views and language-model commonsense estimates. The paper is strongest as a systems contribution, but its automation and scalability claims would benefit from end-to-end success rate, failure taxonomy, throughput, and compute/API-cost measurements.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the work is most naturally assessed as Applied/Systems: its main value is the integration of instance generation, alignment, physics-enabled assembly, editing, trajectory synthesis, and real-robot deployment into one automated pipeline. Under that framing, the end-to-end scope and practical problem are meaningful.

The independent-object representation is useful for manipulation because it supports collision geometry, object-level interaction, and add/remove/replace/rearrange operations. The reported collision and settling results are substantially better than those of the evaluated baselines.

The evaluation is broad in presentation, including 78 image-conditioned scenes, text-conditioned comparisons, component ablations, a 126-participant user study, additional recent baselines, and three real-robot policy-transfer tasks with 50 trials each. The 68–84% real-world success rates provide encouraging evidence that the generated environments can support simple manipulation.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. The pipeline, DRO objective, camera-sweep protocol, intermediate outputs, prompts, and qualitative comparisons are presented accessibly.
weaknesses: The core TSA method is too under-specified to constitute a reproducible technical contribution. Equation (5) only defines anchor selection; the paper does not formally specify how the metric scale, per-object scales, translations, support relations, or collision-free layout are computed afterward. The supplementary description mainly says that bounding-box coordinates and ChatGPT estimates are used. There is no explicit optimization or collision-resolution procedure supporting the claimed globally consistent and physically plausible recovery.

The evaluation set is highly synthetic and potentially circular: 74 of 78 inputs are generated images, while only four are real photographs, and the proposed pipeline itself relies on Seedream for reference-image synthesis, instance completion, and top-view synthesis. Performance on images produced by the same generative ecosystem provides weak evidence of robustness to real, cluttered, occluded, or out-of-distribution tabletop observations.

The paper does not measure actual reconstruction accuracy. There are no ground-truth rotation, translation, scale, geometry, support-relation, or object-completeness errors. LPIPS, DINOv2, CLIP, and GPT judgments of selected renderings cannot establish metric layout correctness, especially because generative completion and top-view synthesis may alter the observed objects and arrangement.

Several comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. The method benefits from per-instance generative completion and a high-quality image-to-3D model, whereas the baselines have different objectives and asset-generation capabilities. Particularly relevant compositional alignment methods such as Reparo are discussed but not directly evaluated. The text-to-scene experiment uses only 30 prompts and largely relies on GPT-4o judgments, with no human evaluation or downstream manipulation comparison.

The GPT-based evaluation lacks essential reproducibility and reliability details, including the exact judging prompt, precise model/version, sampling parameters, repeated-run variance, and measures against positional or self-preference bias. Despite repeated claims of significant or overwhelming improvements, neither the automatic metrics nor the user-study results include confidence intervals or statistical tests.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed design choices. Removing DRO or TSA means replacing the component with a ChatGPT estimate, which tests specialized processing against a weak prompt baseline rather than validating the specific formulation. There are no ablations of the three DRO losses, RMA anchor selection, synthesized top view, stacking prior, camera estimation, or commonsense-size estimates.

The real-to-sim-to-real study is promising but too narrow to validate the paper's broad data-engine claims. It uses one reconstructed setup, three simple tasks, and no comparison against alternative reconstruction systems, real-data training, or policies trained without the proposed alignment. Thus, success cannot be attributed specifically to TabletopGen rather than domain randomization, the pretrained policy, or task-specific choices.

Physical realism is only partially demonstrated. Collision, support, and five-second settling tests do not verify collision-shape accuracy, mass, friction, center of mass, graspability, articulation, or contact behavior. The manuscript does not explain how physical parameters are selected, yet makes broad claims about reliable physical properties and executable environments.

The claimed scalability is not quantified: there are no runtime, compute, monetary cost, API dependence, success/failure rate, throughput, or manual-intervention measurements. Reliance on unspecified versions of proprietary ChatGPT and Seedream services further limits reproducibility. Overall, the system is ambitious and visually compelling, but consequential gaps in method specification, evaluation independence, and causal downstream validation leave the scientific case below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than purely Algorithms/General: the main value is a complete, automated pipeline that turns text or one image into an instance-level, physics-enabled tabletop scene and uses it for manipulation-data generation.

The system addresses a practically important gap between visually plausible 3D scene generation and simulation-ready environments. Independent objects, collision geometry, physical settling, scene editing, motion planning, and multimodal trajectory collection form a compelling end-to-end package.

The decoupled alignment design is sensible. DRO combines silhouette, contour, and appearance evidence for yaw estimation, while TSA incorporates top-view layout and support relations. The ablation shows that removing TSA increases scene collision rate from 7.69% to 61.54%, with additional degradation when both stages are removed.

The empirical evaluation is broad for a systems paper: 78 image-conditioned scenes, text-conditioned comparisons, several recent baselines, perceptual metrics, collision measurements, support and dynamic-settling tests, qualitative results, and a 126-response human study. TabletopGen achieves particularly strong physical results, including 0.42% colliding object pairs, 100% support stability, and 92.13% dynamic-settling stability.

The real-robot study materially strengthens the paper. Policies trained using 2,000 synthetic demonstrations per task attain 84%, 80%, and 68% success over 50 real-world trials for three tasks, showing that the generated environments can support more than visual rendering.
The paper is clearly organized and visually convincing. The supplementary material exposes intermediate outputs, prompts, evaluation protocols, and user-study procedures, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The evaluation distribution is narrow relative to the generalization claims: 74 of the 78 inputs are synthesized images and only four are real photographs. Because Seedream is used both to create reference images and to synthesize TSA top views, the reported performance may substantially reflect an unusually favorable, internally consistent generative distribution.

The main geometric mechanism is evaluated mostly through downstream visual similarity and physical-validity metrics. There is no dataset with ground-truth object pose, metric scale, support graph, or tabletop layout, so claims of accurate pose and scale recovery are not directly established.

The ablation does not isolate several important design choices, including the three DRO loss terms, generated top view versus alternatives, stacking priors, commonsense-size estimation, RMA anchor selection, or global versus per-object scaling. Replacing an entire stage with an MLLM estimate demonstrates utility but provides limited attribution of the improvement.

The visual protocol selects the best of 160 rendered views independently using similarity to the input, which can inflate scores and does not directly test camera or layout recovery. Mean-view results are reassuring but are reported only against MIDI rather than all baselines.

The downstream validation covers three tasks in apparently one reconstructed tabletop setting and lacks a control using scenes produced by a competing reconstruction method or simpler manually built simulation. Thus, it demonstrates feasibility but does not fully establish that TabletopGen's scene-generation advances cause the policy-transfer gains.

Reproducibility remains uncertain because major components are proprietary or version-dependent, including ChatGPT and Seedream, while physical-property assignment, collision-decomposition settings, runtime, compute cost, failure rate, and retry policy are insufficiently specified. The text also cites Hunyuan3D-2.5 while stating that Hunyuan3D-3.0 is used.

DRO itself is a fairly standard differentiable-rendering optimization, and TSA depends on hallucinated top views and MLLM commonsense sizes that may fail for uncommon objects, severe occlusion, or ambiguous support relations. Failure cases and robustness to these errors are not analyzed.

The scope is limited to rigid-object tabletop pick-and-place scenes; articulated objects, deformables, liquids, drawers, cabinets, and more complex contact-rich manipulation are not supported. This is a reasonable scope, but some broad data-engine and generalization language should be moderated.
